targets.text: Culture Nodes owns a ticket end to end across hosts: work crosses a machine boundary as a portable handle, a deadline stops the session it bounds, and the run explains itself without a companion document.

Every one of the three verbs in the announcement is demonstrated against a LIVE cross-host run, not a test: a byte crosses spark->thor through an artifact handle, a deadline stops a real actor session, and a reader reconstructs that run from the run alone. If any of the three is only unit-tested, the announcement is overstated and must be narrowed to what was actually run.

An artifact Put/Get API route, persisted InvocationResult.artifact_refs, and a runner-boundary resolution path are the blocking prerequisite for every other capability in #87. internal/artifacts is a complete library (Store, Router, ref.go's artifact://<namespace>/<id> scheme, postgres + s3 drivers, migrations 0004_observability.sql + 0006_artifact_blobs.sql) with ZERO production callers: grepping the import across the tree returns only its own tests and drivers, and internal/api/server.go's route table (lines 300-346) registers no artifact route.

The artifact path is proven by a node on ONE host writing what a node on a DIFFERENT host reads — not by a same-host round trip, and not by a unit test against the Store interface. A same-host proof does not distinguish a working artifact path from a shared filesystem.

AMENDED after the q9 decision — this boundary as originally written was FALSE, and its own honesty condition h17 is what caught it. The original text said the fix->review handoff contract was already shipped and enforced and must not be redesigned, citing tests/lint/crosshosthandoff_test.go's requirement that fix.completed carry an artifact:// handle. h17 pinned that boundary to 'the guard passes UNCHANGED after the artifact path lands; if implementing the mechanism requires editing the guard, the contract was not settled and this boundary is false.' The q9 decision requires exactly that edit, so the antecedent holds and the boundary is retired. What SURVIVES and is still binding: the guard's refusal of a bare filesystem path between nodes whose actors may differ (the 403-that-names-authorization-when-the-cause-is-topology failure), the closed missing_capability enum on handoff_unavailable, and the rule that handoff_unavailable never routes into review. What CHANGES: handoff.kind gains git_ref beside artifact, and the guard asserts a portable handle of EITHER kind rather than an artifact:// specifically.

After the change, tests/lint/crosshosthandoff_test.go still REFUSES a bare filesystem path handed between nodes — verified by a case that hands one and expects rejection. That refusal is the load-bearing half of the guard and the thing #74 was actually about; widening the accepted handle kinds must not weaken it. Supersedes the rejected h17, whose antecedent the q9 decision satisfied.

A node deadline cannot stop an actor session today for a STRUCTURAL reason, not an oversight: the expiry runs in internal/scheduler (scheduler.go:688 deadlineTimeoutOutput, waitForDeadlineTimer at :617), and the Scheduler struct holds only db, pool, opts, and a per-namespace engine cache — no actors.Client and no actor Registry, so the process that expires the timer has no way to address a bridge. Wiring one in is proven three times over: internal/api/cancelpropagate.go builds its own worker.NewDBRegistry plus a package-level actors.NewClient(), internal/worker/branchcancel.go does it for reaped branches, and internal/worker/budget.go's cancelPendingInvocation does it for budget exhaustion — resolve the pending invocation, resolve the endpoint, Cancel best-effort, record an event, swallow every failure.

The deadline's cancel is verified by observing the ACTOR SESSION end — a process gone, a callback arriving, a provider thread closed — never by reading the run's status back. #87 acceptance 3 names this distinction explicitly, and reading the status back is exactly the bookkeeping fiction the issue is about.

Preserve-on-failure cannot be fixed engine-side alone. It is BRIDGE-side and triggered by a failure the bridge itself observes: adapters/claude-code/src/claude_code_bridge/server.py:538-555 and adapters/codex/src/codex_bridge/async_runner.py:263-277 both call preserve.preserve_on_failure() on their own technical-failure path and attach the result under a 'preserve' key. On a deadline expiry the ENGINE gives up while the bridge session keeps running, so the bridge never reaches its failure path and preserve never fires — which is exactly the mechanism behind #78's 'preserve_branch: None'. This makes #78 a consequence of #82: once the deadline's cancel actually reaches the bridge, the cancellation becomes a bridge-observed terminal event it can preserve from. Fixing #78 without #82 would require a second, independent preservation path.

A test pins the DEADLINE path specifically, with a dirty workspace, and asserts a preserve ref exists. The existing preserve tests were mutation-verified on two bridges but never against a deadline expiry — which is precisely how this gap survived a high-confidence delivery claim.

The API genuinely does not expose attempt attribution, and this half of #77 is confirmed rather than inferred. api/openapi/openapi.json's Attempt schema has exactly: actor_id, attempt_number, completed_at, fencing_token, id, node_run_id, preserve_branch, preserve_pushed, preserve_remote, result, started_at, status. No usage, no usage_model, no termination_reason, no continuation_ref. A live GET /v1alpha1/runs/{id} accordingly returns usage=null on every attempt including a succeeded claude-developer attempt from today — which means the API as it stands CANNOT distinguish 'the column is null' from 'the API does not render it'. Surfacing the usage block on the Attempt schema is a precondition for even measuring whether the write path works.

Adding usage to the Attempt schema is done in the OpenAPI document AND the Go handler AND the run-detail page together, so a reader never has one surface claiming a fact another cannot show. A schema change alone leaves the same measurement blindness in place under a new name.

colleague and notify are the real all-backends gap in #77. adapters/colleague/mapping.py:234-249 maps prompt/completion tokens and its docstring states that cost, currency, cache, reasoning, model and thread fields are 'omitted, never zero-filled'; adapters/notify has no mapping.py usage surface at all. #77 asks for absence recorded as an explicit unknown rather than a null indistinguishable from 'nobody wrote it' — for these two backends that is the whole of the work, and it needs a representation for 'this backend cannot report a model' that the ledger can tell apart from 'not measured'.

colleague and notify report an EXPLICIT unknown that the ledger can distinguish from 'not measured' — a rollup grouping tokens by model must be able to tell 'this backend cannot say' apart from 'nobody wrote it'. A null serves neither, which is the whole of #77's complaint.

adapters/*/preflight.py is BYTE-IDENTICAL across all four bridges — md5 76e595f6, 339 lines, in claude-code, codex, colleague and notify. So #83's fix is one edit applied four times in lockstep, and the all-backends rule here is literal file duplication rather than four independent implementations. tests/lint/preflightsurface_test.go already exists as the guard over this surface.

All four preflight.py copies stay byte-identical after the change — verified by comparing digests, not by intent. They are identical today (md5 76e595f6); a change that lands in three of four is exactly the all-backends bug CLAUDE.md names.

#83's contradiction is real and one doctrine must lose in writing. preflight.py's userns_restrictions() docstring states 'the sysctls ARE the fact, so read them rather than shelling out to bwrap to find out', while deploy/prod/README.md and codex-preflight.sh check 7 state 'Verify by capability, never by reading the sysctl back. The value says what was configured; only the probe says what works.' The second was established by probing during the #63 fix. Whichever wins, the loser's prose changes in the same diff — leaving both standing is how the next reader picks the wrong one.

The losing doctrine's prose is edited in the SAME diff that changes the measurement. Leaving both 'the sysctls ARE the fact' and 'verify by capability, never by reading the sysctl back' standing is how the next reader picks the wrong one, and the contradiction is the actual defect #83 reports.

#84 is WORSE on the host than it was filed, verified by reading spark's live systemd user units rather than the deploy script. There are THREE config mechanisms for one bridge, not two: (1) the running culture-nodes-human-inbox.service uses Environment=HUMAN_INBOX_BRIDGE_CONFIG=%h/.config/culture-nodes-bridges/human-ops.json — a JSON config file, with NO EnvironmentFile at all; (2) the running culture-nodes-human-inbox-tracker.service uses EnvironmentFile=%h/.config/culture-nodes-bridges/human-ops-tracker.env; (3) deploy.sh (lines 386-430) writes ~/.culture-nodes/human-inbox-bridge.env and ~/.culture-nodes/human-inbox-tracker.env and installs units named human-inbox-bridge.service / human-inbox-tracker.service that read ~/.culture-nodes/human-inbox-bridge.env plus ~/.culture-nodes/human-inbox.env. Reconciling 'the env-file path' as the issue frames it is not enough; a JSON-config bridge and an EnvironmentFile bridge are different configuration contracts.

The deploy is proven by running it twice against a host that already has the OTHER naming installed, and observing adoption rather than a port conflict on both runs. A single clean-host run proves nothing about the case this issue is entirely about.

The production claude-code bridges on spark run FROM THIS WORKING TREE: culture-nodes-claude-developer.service (and intake/planner/verifier) declare WorkingDirectory=/home/spark/git/culture-nodes/adapters/claude-code and ExecStart=uv run claude-code-bridge. Editing adapter source in this checkout changes production bridge behaviour on the next restart, with no deploy step in between. Any work on adapters/ during this cycle has to treat that as a live surface — and it is also the reason the model-attribution plumbing from b5cdc5b is already deployed on spark's claude bridges without anyone deploying it.

Any adapter change in this batch is followed by a deliberate restart of the four spark bridges, or it is not in effect. The corollary is the sharper half: an adapter edit is live on next restart whether or not anyone intended a deploy, so the batch must never leave adapters/ in a half-edited state across a restart boundary.

#86 part A is mechanically small and the inputs are already in hand: deploy/prod/deploy.sh:30-31 already does git rev-parse --short $BRANCH and ships git archive of that same revision, and lines 68-75 take PR_UPKEEP_SWEEP_SOURCE_URL and PR_UPKEEP_SWEEP_SOURCE_SHA256 from the operator's environment, skipping the lane with a named warning when either is unset. Deriving both from the revision being deployed is a change confined to that one lane, and it removes the class of failure where a squash merge orphans the pinned commit.

The derived pin is proven against a SQUASH-MERGED revision — the exact case that orphaned commit 0abf042 — not against a branch tip that happens to still be reachable. The current pin also 'works' right now, which is why testing the happy path proves nothing.

#86 part B must move the repo pin from a code literal to a GRANTED environment value resolved by the runner, never to run input — and the guard that enforces this will fail loudly and deliberately. tests/test_pr_upkeep_sweep.py:660-740's TestTheSweptRepoIsPinnedAndSaysSo asserts the module's environment reads are EXACTLY {GITHUB_TOKEN, PR_UPKEEP_MAX_PRS_PER_SWEEP, PR_UPKEEP_REQUIRED_CHECKS} and that SONAR_COMPONENT_KEY and GITHUB_REPO are plain literals, with an error message that says a new read naming a repo or component key 'is the boundary this example refuses to make configurable'. Editing that set is the deliberate act the issue asks for; the blast-radius note at examples/pr-upkeep/sweep.py:85-93 gets rewritten in the same diff rather than deleted.

The swept repo remains unreachable from run input after the change — a caller naming a repo in a workflow field or run input must still be refused. tests/test_pr_upkeep_sweep.py's environment-read assertion is edited deliberately to admit exactly the new granted value and nothing more, and the blast-radius note is rewritten rather than deleted.

The dependency order is forced by the mechanics, not chosen — and it has been re-threaded twice, by the q6 and q9 decisions. (1) TWO PARALLEL UNBLOCKING TRACKS, because the q9 decision gives the handoff two carriers: the ARTIFACT track is #79 (route, persisted artifact_refs, runner-boundary resolution, and its authorization model q5 settled BEFORE the route is built), carrying context and data; the GIT-REF track is the bridge push credential (c70) plus reuse of t25's write-tree/commit-tree/update-ref machinery, carrying a runner's changes. The pr-upkeep reference case needs BOTH — the sweep's item list is context, the fix's diff is changes — so neither track alone completes it. (2) A MINIMAL SLICE OF #80 next: the continue.while declaration, its compilation and its CEL evaluation, because the q6 decision makes the deadline consult it AND the q7/c63 decision makes a failed handover gate route to it. This is a reversal of the pre-challenge order, which had #80 after #78 and #77. (3) #82: the post-commit cancel (q3/c48), the workspace fence (c49), the late-callback reconciliation (c37), a deadline-cancel event type (c46). (4) #78 falls out of #82 plus honest-absence reporting — and its push leg is fixed by c70 on the git-ref track. (5) #77's API surface, then #28's model-attributed grades, then the rest of #80. Parallel throughout, touching nothing the chain edits: #83 (adapters/preflight.py), #84 (deploy/prod/ — composes with c70's credential work), #86 (examples/pr-upkeep/). #81 and #76 last.

The no-model-in-the-control-plane rule is enforced by a tests/lint gate, the way webhookisolation_test.go and github_isolation_test.go already enforce their boundaries — not by a comment or a review convention. #81 states this as acceptance, and an unenforced boundary in this repo has a track record of drifting.

#86's knock-on (part D) is confirmed exact-match, not prefix: adapters/claude-code/src/claude_code_bridge/config.py:196-201 resolves the requested repo and returns 'resolved in self.repo_allowlist'. So sweeping N repos requires N checkouts AND N allowlist entries on the fix actor's host, and the same again on the review actor's host — otherwise the sweep surfaces findings for repos the fix node is refused from touching, and the refusal (a correct 403) arrives one node too late. Sizing the configured repo set is therefore a per-host provisioning cost, not a config-file edit.

Every repo in the configured set has a checkout AND an exact-match allowlist entry on BOTH the fix and review actor hosts before the set is enlarged. config.py:196-201 is an exact-match membership test on a resolved path, so a missing entry surfaces as a correct 403 one node too late to be useful.

Session accounting binds this batch's shape, per CLAUDE.md's economy lane and issue #48. The operator's interactive Claude session, local subagents, and every bridge session on the same account share ONE subscription window. Eleven issues is not a wave; whatever subset is chosen needs a declared model-session count per wave against the remaining window before any fan-out, with big analysis/build packages routed to codex actors and the operator's window reserved for operator-lane work and merge gates.

The split plan declares an expected model-session count per wave against the REMAINING subscription window before any assignment, and the operator's own window is reserved for operator-lane work and merge gates. Issue #47's diagnosis is that a fan-out which does not do this exhausts the window mid-wave — this batch is larger than the one that did.

#78's evidence is stronger on the timeout path and WEAKER on the failure path than either the issue or my first reading of the data claimed. Measured on thor: preserve_branch is NULL on all 140 attempts, but the sample that could have exercised the failure path since t25 shipped (b5cdc5b, 2026-08-14) is ZERO. Only 2 of 13 failed attempts were on agent actors at all, and both predate t25 — one is retryable_transport (the invocation never reached the bridge, so no bridge-side preserve could have run by construction) and one is an execution failure from 2026-08-12. So the database neither confirms nor refutes the failure path; it has never been exercised in production. What IS established: 5 timed_out attempts, zero preserve branches, and — separately — every one of those 5 has a NULL actor_id, including 01M00DACGHSZ2QD73G5YA75N4V from today. The delivery claim in docs/deliveries/2026-08-14-economy-discord-graphs.md should be rescoped to 'verified by test, never exercised in production' rather than either 'high confidence' or 'false'.

The delivery-claim correction states what was actually verified and what was not: preserve-on-failure is verified BY TEST on two bridges and has never been exercised in production on any path. Restating it as either 'high confidence' or 'false' would both be wrong, and the correction is worthless if it is not more precise than the claim it replaces.

v1 is resolved and it makes #78 a consequence of #82 rather than independent work. Reading adapters/codex/src/codex_bridge/async_runner.py:201-278: cancel() sends SIGTERM cooperatively and never SIGKILL; _run() measures the workspace unconditionally after the session ends whatever ended it; a cancelled session is classified as incomplete rather than success, so it produces a 'failed' terminal event; and a 'failed' terminal event routes through preserve.preserve_on_failure BEFORE the terminal callback fires. The claude-code bridge carries the same hook on both its sync (server.py:543) and async (async_runner.py:192) paths, and preserve_on_failure defaults True with none of spark's five bridge configs overriding it. So the preservation window #78 asks for already exists — wiring the deadline to Cancel (#82) makes a timed-out node's work preserve through the path that is already built, with no second preservation mechanism. The residual #78 work is the honest-absence reporting (preserve_attempted:false with a reason) and a test that pins the deadline path specifically.

The claim that a cancelled session reaches preserve is verified by RUNNING one — cancel a live session with a dirty workspace and observe the preserve branch — not only by reading async_runner.py's ordering. Code reading established the path exists; only a run establishes it fires.

Three audiences, in the order the work serves them. (1) The OPERATOR running a development cycle through Culture Nodes — today they are the transport (copying bytes between hosts), the memory (writing the state file the ledger could not), and the recovery mechanism (committing a timed-out node's work by hand). (2) A READER WHO WAS NOT PRESENT — a reviewer, a future maintainer, or the same operator six weeks later — who must reconstruct what happened from the run alone. (3) The AGENT FLEET itself, which needs work to cross a host boundary and needs its own attempts attributed well enough that the comparative record means something.

Each of the three audiences has at least one success signal in c35 that would fail if their need went unmet. An audience nothing measures is decoration — if the reader-who-was-not-present has no falsifiable signal, that audience is aspirational and should be struck rather than claimed.

After this batch: work crosses a machine boundary as an artifact:// handle resolved through the store, with no path passed between nodes and no operator copy step — the pr-upkeep fix->review handoff completes across spark and thor. A node that exceeds its deadline has its actor session STOPPED, and its in-flight work lands on a preserve branch through the path that already exists, recoverable without a human touching a filesystem. Every attempt records which model ran it, at what effort, at what cost, and the Attempt API surface carries that so it can be read without a database. A run explains itself: what was asked, what ran it, what it produced, what was measured versus claimed, and why it ended as it did, with no companion document. The human acts at the three devague gates and at ledger promotion, and nowhere else.

Every verb in the after-state is demonstrated on a LIVE run rather than a test: bytes actually cross spark to thor, a real session is actually stopped, a real run is actually read without a companion file. Any verb only unit-tested is narrowed in the delivery summary to what was run — this repo has already shipped one high-confidence claim (preserve-on-failure) that was true by test and never exercised in production.

Before: the 2026-08-14 upkeep-actors-jira cycle cost five specific things, each a record rather than a hypothetical. A human rescued the filesystem — run 01M00BKCVT04SSGPNXDF3JJX5G was recorded failed while its session kept working and committed 3f9bd3c, which survived only because a person looked. Work could not cross ANY boundary — run 01M00NVQH582QBARWSYFR0WTG1 swept successfully and terminated at handoff_unavailable because a code node's output is runner metadata and no artifact route is mounted. The rescue path does not work on the host it was built for — the spark bridge service cannot push. The ledger cannot say who did the work — 1 of 140 attempts records a model, and that one only because a bridge restarted onto new code an hour before. And the record needed a companion document to be legible: docs/deliveries/2026-08-14-upkeep-actors-jira-STATE.md exists, and its existence IS the evidence.

Every one of the five costs cites a run id, a commit, a measured count or a committed file that a reader can check independently. A before-state built from recollection rather than records is the exact failure the companion-document problem is about, and would be self-refuting here.

The human is meant to be the DECIDER, not the plumbing and not the memory. Every hour spent copying bytes between hosts, re-reading a worktree to find out whether a failed run actually failed, or writing down what the ledger could not say, is an hour not spent on the only judgement a human is uniquely needed for. The dogfooding reflex in CLAUDE.md exists to accumulate a comparative record of which actor is better at what — and every grade in that record currently rates an ENDPOINT against an unknown model, so the evidence is weaker than it reads. Fixing that is not tidiness; it is what makes the accumulated record worth anything.

The claim that grades currently rate an endpoint against an unknown model is checkable against the ledger: the two grade records from this cycle (ledger_01M0085GSDSXNQKEKK4WCXM6FX, ledger_01M008J5468R4T4WVH2D14WX9C) name no model, and usage_model was NULL on every attempt before 17:45 today. If a later reading contradicts that, this rationale weakens and must be restated.

Six falsifiable signals, each demonstrable or failable, taken from #87's acceptance and sharpened by what the scope probes established. (1) A node killed mid-write has its session stopped and its work recovered from the run alone, with no filesystem access — provable because the preserve path already fires on a cancelled session. (2) The pr-upkeep fix->review handoff completes across two machines with no path passed and no operator copy step. (3) Cancelling a run ends the actor session, verified by observing the session end rather than reading the run status. (4) usage_model coverage moves from 1/140 to every fresh attempt on all four backends, with colleague and notify reporting an explicit unknown rather than a null. (5) The companion-document test: this cycle's -STATE.md would not have needed to exist, measured as a diff against what the delivery_summary projection renders. (6) A cycle of this shape completes with the human acting only at the three devague gates and at ledger promotion.

Every signal is falsifiable BEFORE the work starts — each names an observation that could come back negative, and none is written so that shipping the code automatically satisfies it. Signal 5 in particular is measured as a diff against what delivery_summary renders versus what the hand-written -STATE.md said, not as an opinion that the run reads well. Any signal that cannot fail is struck rather than counted, which is how last cycle's signal 5 became unverifiable.

This batch does not weaken PRD 10.4 and does not make the merge gate machine-DECIDED. Agents create only proposed records; humans confirm or reject; no actor promotes its own proposal; an agent saying 'done' stays a completion claim rather than evidence. The merge gate may become machine-VERIFIED — measured diffs, an independent review step, observed workspace evidence — but whether a machine may decide a merge is a separate question this work does not answer. The three devague gates stay. The work removes the human from TRANSPORT and RECALL, never from decision.

No record created by an agent in this batch lands with any authority above 'proposed', and no code path lets an actor promote its own proposal — checkable by the existing ledger authority tests rather than by review. If the batch needs an exception to ship a capability, that is a signal the capability is designed wrong, not that the boundary should move.

Wiring the deadline to Cancel is NOT sufficient on its own, and this binds #82, #78 and #77 into one change. The bridge's terminal event — carrying the preserve block AND the usage/model block for the work that actually happened — arrives after the engine has committed the attempt as timed_out. That makes it a LATE callback, and internal/actors/callback.go:748-755's late() records a TypeCallbackLate event and calls CloseInvocation(superseded), writing NOTHING to the attempts table. So the preserve branch would exist in git and stay invisible in the ledger (preserve_branch still NULL), and the model that did the work would stay unrecorded — exactly the two gaps #78 and #77 are about. #82's second ask — a late terminal callback reconciled as a superseding record rather than dropped — is therefore the CARRIER for the other two fixes, not a nicety. NOTE (amended after the challenge pass): this claim originally also required the Cancel to be issued BEFORE CompleteAttempt commits. That ordering is SUPERSEDED by the q3 decision — it collided with the scheduler's transaction shape (c40) and would not have closed the re-dispatch race anyway (c42). The cancel now goes out after commit and the race is closed by a workspace fence. The late-callback reconciliation is unaffected and remains required.

The late-callback reconciliation is proven by a superseding attempt record that actually carries the preserve branch and the usage/model block — read back from the attempts table, not from a TypeCallbackLate event body. An event-only trace is exactly the invisibility this claim identifies, so a fix that only enriches the event has not fixed it.

CHALLENGE / adjacent-systems lens: the superseding attempt record c37 requires would RE-CREATE, one layer down, the exact actor-scoring distortion #82 exists to fix. Two facts collide. (1) migrations/0002_runtime_execution.sql:71 declares CONSTRAINT attempts_node_run_attempt_number_key UNIQUE (node_run_id, attempt_number), and engine_store.go:659 mints the next number as MAX(attempt_number)+1 — so a superseding record CANNOT reuse the timed-out attempt's number and must take a new one. (2) actorstats.go:373-376's loadActorRetryBurnAttempts counts 'every attempt this actor made, in scope, REGARDLESS of its technical outcome — a retried, failed attempt still counts', and ActorRetryBurn is #28's headline 'attempts per completion' quality measure. So every deadline reconciliation would add a second attempt row for one dispatch and inflate that actor's retry burn — penalising the actor for the engine's own late bookkeeping, which is precisely #82 point 1's complaint ('any per-actor analytics built on run status will score this actor as having failed a task it completed') reappearing in a new place. The supersession representation must be excluded from retry-burn counting, or carried somewhere other than a second attempts row.

The supersession representation is proven not to move an actor's retry burn: read GET /v1alpha1/actors/{id}/stats before and after a deadline reconciliation and assert Attempts is unchanged. A fix that merely 'looks right' in the schema reintroduces #82 point 1's distortion in the metric #28 exists to provide.

CHALLENGE / concurrency+operations lens: decision c38 puts a network cancel inside an OPEN POSTGRES TRANSACTION on a SERIAL, SINGLETON loop, and that is an availability hazard on the exact path meant to make timeouts reliable. scheduler.go:386-420's fireOne opens tx, calls applyEffect (where the deadline effect and therefore the new cancel would sit), and only then does MarkFiredTx + InsertOutboxTx + commit; scheduler.go:355-362's tick iterates the claimed batch SERIALLY ('for _, t := range due { _ = sch.fireOne(ctx, t) }') with a default batch size of 100; and only one instance is active at a time behind the advisory lock. #21 measured a codex-bridge cancel at ~2.2s idle and >10s mid-session, and every existing Cancel caller allows 30s. So a handful of expired deadlines against one slow or unreachable bridge stalls ALL timer firing for the whole deployment — wait timers, retry timers and lease recovery included. Note applyEffect's own comment already establishes the pattern for stepping outside tx (the deadline and lease-recovery effects deliberately use the ambient pool), but the cancel would still block fireOne's transaction because applyEffect is called inside it.

The scheduler's tick latency is measured with a deliberately unreachable bridge holding expired deadlines, and stays bounded — proven by a test or a probe, not by the cancel having moved out of the transaction on paper. The q3 decision removes the stall by construction, so this condition is what confirms the construction is actually what shipped.

CHALLENGE / security lens: #79's artifact route has NO usable authentication model today, and the critical path runs straight through it. internal/actors/token.go is strictly attempt-scoped — the signed payload is exactly (attempt id, expiry), VerifyFor refuses 'a valid token for a different attempt', and DefaultTokenTTL is 15 minutes. Two consequences neither #79 nor #74 names. (a) CROSS-ATTEMPT READ: the review node on thor must GET an artifact produced by the fix node's attempt on spark, but its own token names its own attempt and nothing else — so the artifact GET cannot reuse the callback-token model as-is. It needs a run-scoped read grant or a per-artifact capability handed to the consuming node at dispatch, and neither seam exists. (b) TTL vs LONG SESSIONS: a token minted at dispatch expires in 15 minutes, while the publish happens at the END of a session that may run to a 30-minute deadline — so the artifact upload is the operation MOST likely to present an expired token, and the timeout case (#82) is exactly where it bites. token.go's own comment says a long-running actor 'is expected to be re-issued a token', which presumes a re-issue path the artifact publish would have to use.

The cross-host handoff is proven with the consuming node presenting only credentials it was legitimately given — no shared secret, no token minted for another attempt, no auth bypass for the artifact route. If the only way to make review read fix's artifact is to weaken the attempt-scoping, the authorization model is wrong and must be redesigned rather than excepted.

CHALLENGE / failure-mode lens: #82's concurrent-writer hazard is not hypothetical and not merely 'possible' — it is LIVE in production today, and the fix for the c40 transaction-stall hazard would make it worse. internal/engine/types.go:261-268's retryable() returns true for StatusFailed, StatusTimedOut AND StatusContractRejected, and complete.go:415 re-dispatches whenever 'c.status.retryable() && c.attemptNumber < c.node.Retry.MaxAttempts'. So ANY node declaring MaxAttempts > 1 whose deadline fires is re-dispatched while the first session is still running and writing to the same workspace. Run 01M00BKCVT04SSGPNXDF3JJX5G escaped this only because that node did not declare a retry. The coupling matters: if the cancel is moved AFTER the commit to avoid stalling the scheduler (c40), then CompleteAttempt commits timed_out, the item becomes immediately retryable, and a second dispatch can begin BEFORE the cancel is even sent. Nothing today gates re-dispatch on cancellation having completed, and nothing fences the workspace against a second writer. Whichever way q2/q3 is decided, one of those two guards has to exist.

A node with MaxAttempts > 1 whose deadline fires is shown to produce exactly ONE writing session — verified by observing the second dispatch being refused, not by observing that no corruption happened to occur. Absence of observed corruption is not evidence of the fence working; this failure mode has no detection, which is why #82 calls it the serious one.

risks.text: Least-privilege posture on the bridge push credential: an unattended service holding a broad token is a larger blast radius than the handover needs. A permissions probe reported admin/push true, but for a fine-grained PAT that reflects the authenticated identity's role rather than the token's grant, so the probe cannot tell a correctly-narrow Contents:write token from a broad classic repo-scope one. Verified at the operator's discretion (a classic PAT is prefixed ghp_, a fine-grained one github_pat_); the remedy if broad is to reissue fine-grained. Not blocking — t1's acceptance criteria carry the check.
risks.resolution: Resolved by measurement, using the new scripts/verify-token-scope.sh: GITHUB_TOKEN_WORKER is type=fine_grained, coarse_scoped=false, oauth_scopes empty (a classic token would return the x-oauth-scopes header), push present on agentculture/culture-nodes, within_policy=true, exit 0. The least-privilege concern is answered: it is not a coarse repo-scope classic token.

risks.text: Routing decided: warm packages, codex-routed. Same-lane tasks group into persistent warm sessions with many ledgered sub-actions (~3-4 packages per wave, not one session per task); big analysis/build packages go to codex-thor and codex-orin so the cold-session tax buys ledger attribution and cross-machine execution; the operator's Claude window is reserved for merge gates only. This implements c24/h15 and the nodes-operator split-plan guidance, and deliberately avoids #47's failure shape (per-task cold sessions plus parallel subagents exhausting one shared window mid-wave). The residual exposure is #18: the codex workspace-write path has never been proven to land a patch, and this routing puts most of the batch's writing on it — wave 0 is therefore also the probe that proves or falsifies it.

h54's separation test is NOT yet satisfied and the API cannot settle it. Measured: GITHUB_TOKEN and GITHUB_TOKEN_WORKER are distinct values (sha256 digests differ) and both are fine-grained, but BOTH report push:true on agentculture/culture-nodes. Per verify-token-scope.sh's own caveat, a repository permissions block reflects the AUTHENTICATED IDENTITY's role rather than the token's grant, so for two tokens owned by an org owner it cannot distinguish a read-only grant from a write one. h54 requires that the sweep FAIL to push when handed only its own token; establishing that needs a non-mutating capability probe the script deliberately does not perform. The right primitive is 'git push --dry-run', which contacts the remote and exercises the permission check without writing — add it to the verification node as an opt-in probe, gated behind an explicit flag so verification stays side-effect-free by default.
risks.resolution: SETTLED by measurement, and h54 is satisfied. Added a write-capability probe to scripts/verify-token-scope.sh: a plain GET of the receive-pack advertisement (https://github.com/<repo>.git/info/refs?service=git-receive-pack), which GitHub gates on the TOKEN's write permission and which has no side effect — no git invocation, no pack negotiation, no ref touched. Results: GITHUB_TOKEN_WORKER returns 200 (can push); the sweep's GITHUB_TOKEN returns 403 (read-only). The separation c73 requires is therefore REAL, not nominal. This also demonstrates why the API alone could not settle it: BOTH tokens report role_implies_push=true from the repository permissions block, because that reflects the owner's role — the measured field disagrees with the role-derived one, and the measured one is authoritative. The script now reports both and says which to believe.
